title: Why OCM matters; making change stick through culture
blurb: Explain why an agile change needs organizational change management, and pick the action that makes it last.
question: At Easterholm County Council, senior managers see agile as a way to dodge accountability and social workers fear their judgement will be bypassed. The director asks what will stop the new ways of working fading once Care Online closes. What is the BEST answer?

teach.body: Organizational change management (OCM) is the means by which an organization moves from its current state to its target state. A project can deliver a working app on time, yet the benefits appear only when people actually work differently. An agile change is a change in how people think and work, not a new tool set: adopting a framework does not by itself make delivery faster or better. OCM is the discipline that leads that shift so it is adopted and kept.

teach.h: OCM: from here to there, and staying there

steps.label: Target state
steps.sub: Agile mindset and values in use

steps.label: Make it stick
steps.sub: Evolve culture so it is not rolled back

teach.caption: The change management approach can describe the target state and the route through interim states (book 4.2.1).

teach.h: Where the route is written down
teach.body: PRINCE2 Project Management recommends a change management approach, and it can be tailored for use outside a project. For an agile change it can define the target organizational state for introducing the agile mindset and values, and how the business moves from the current state through interim states. It is agreed in initiating a project. For a single pilot, update this approach. If an agile transformation plan exists for wider adoption, it can replace the change management approach in the project initiation workshop.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1, 2.7.1, Tables 13.6 and 13.7

teach.caption: None of these is change control, which handles baseline changes in the issues practice.

teach.h: What to weigh when setting the detail
head: Consideration (4.2.1)
What it gives you
rows: People hear and are heard about the change
People can work in the new way
The change lasts after the project ends
teach.caption: All three matter. When a question asks what makes the change LAST, the answer is the evolving culture.

teach.h: Culture is what makes it last
teach.body: Doing agile (frameworks, ceremonies, terms) gives short-term efficiency; being agile creates the cultural shift and long-term resilience. So rules, bonuses or a launch message can start a change, but if shared values and habits stay the same, people drift back when the project team leaves. Incentives alone cannot guarantee change stays: balance tangible rewards with purpose, recognition and personal values. People also need more than information: theory training plus coaching on the job.

teach.h: Will this make the change last?

teach.body: Easterholm has never used agile; leaders expect detailed plans approved in advance, and social workers fear online self-assessment bypasses their judgement. Project manager Simon Archer treats Care Online as the council's agile pilot. In initiating a project he updates the change management approach: current state (phone front door, fixed plans), an interim state (practitioners join sprints for research and testing), the target state, and how the ten social workers trained as product champions and on-the-job coaching from agile coach Gita Bhatt will keep the new ways after closure.

teach.caption: Each one brings users closer to the product, so adoption is smoother and faster.

teach.text: Classic trap: making change stick is NOT compliance, money or communication alone; it is evolving the culture. And keep the three terms apart: OCM is the discipline, the change management approach is the project's product, the agile transformation plan covers wider adoption (not needed yet for a single pilot). None of them is change control.

items: OCM moves an organization from its current state to a target state (4.2.1).
Benefits need people to work differently; delivering products is not enough.
The change management approach sets the target state and interim states; agreed in initiation.
Pilot: update the change management approach; wider adoption: agile transformation plan.
Lasting change = evolving culture; incentives, mandates or messages alone do not hold it.
Train AND coach on the job; use frequent releases, demos and feedback to help adoption.

summary: You can now explain why an agile change needs organizational change management, where its route is recorded, and why evolving the culture, not compliance or incentives alone, is what stops the change being rolled back. You can also tell OCM, the change management approach and the agile transformation plan apart in a scenario.

A.q: At Easterholm County Council, the director of adult social services says the digital team will build Care Online in sprints anyway, so she cannot see why the project needs organizational change management. Which statement BEST explains why OCM matters here?
options: Benefits depend on staff and carers adopting new ways of working
OCM sets the tolerances the board uses to control the grant spend
OCM replaces the full business case when a project is an agile pilot
OCM controls requests to change the baselined project backlog items
A.why: OCM is how the organization moves from its current to its target state. Care Online only realizes benefits if social workers, the front door team and carers actually use and support the new way of working (book 4.2.1).

whyNot.1: Tolerances are set through the progress practice and directing, not through OCM.
whyNot.2: The business case (project canvas) is still needed; OCM does not replace it.
whyNot.3: Requests to change baselined project backlog items are handled through change control in the issues practice, not OCM.

A.q: Pinewick Home and Garden has used agile only in its e-commerce team. For the click and collect project, the project manager wants to describe how store teams will move from email reporting and manual stock checks to agile ways of working, through some interim steps. Where should this be described?
options: The communication management approach
The commercial management approach
The change management approach
The quality management approach
A.why: The change management approach can define the target organizational state for introducing the agile mindset and values, and how the business moves from the current state through interim states (book 4.2.1, Table 4.1).

whyNot.0: The communication management approach covers the means and frequency of communication and feedback, not the route to the target state.
whyNot.1: The commercial management approach covers procurement and contracts, such as the Tallis agreement.
whyNot.3: The quality management approach covers quality standards and agile behaviours, not the organizational transition.

A.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group has used agile once, for its website. The board treats Repairs Reimagined as a pilot for agile ways of working, and no wider adoption programme exists yet. The chief executive asks how the move to agile working should be planned for this project. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Write an agile transformation plan before initiation starts
Record the move to agile working in the project canvas
Plan the move to agile working in the project risk register
Update the change management approach for the project
A.why: For a single pilot, an agile transformation plan may not be needed yet; the change management approach is updated to describe the target state and interim states (book 2.7.1, 4.2.1).

whyNot.0: An agile transformation plan typically spans several initiatives for wider adoption; a single pilot does not need one yet.
whyNot.1: The project canvas is the business justification (vision, value, options, costs, benefits, risks), not the change route.
whyNot.2: The risk register records risks; it does not describe the organizational transition.

B.q: In Easterholm's project initiation workshop, agile coach Gita Bhatt explains that the council has now approved a three-year plan to adopt agile across adult social care, children's services and housing, with goals linked to the council's strategy. How can this be reflected in Care Online's management approaches?
options: The Agilometer replaces the change management approach
The agile transformation plan replaces the change management approach
The agile transformation plan replaces the communication approach
The three-year goals are recorded as benefits in the project canvas
B.why: In the project initiation workshop, the agile transformation plan can replace the change management approach if needed (Table 13.7). It holds high-level goals aligned to strategy across several initiatives (2.7.1).

whyNot.0: The Agilometer is a risk tool assessed in the same workshop; it does not describe the organizational change.
whyNot.2: The transformation plan can stand in for the change management approach, not the communication management approach.
whyNot.3: Council-wide adoption goals are not this project's measurable benefits, so they do not belong in its project canvas.

B.q: At Larkspur Rail, the head of customer relations fears automatic payment will change her team's jobs. A board member suggests the team will adapt on its own once Release 3 is live. While the project manager sets the detail of the change management approach, which consideration is MOST important for making the change last?
options: The evolving culture and ways to stop changes being rolled back
The communication strategy for announcing each of the releases
The learning and upskilling needed by the claims-checking team
The stage tolerances the board will set for the later releases
B.why: Book 4.2.1 lists the evolving culture and ways to ensure changes are not rolled back after the transformation; that is what keeps the change in place once the project has gone.

whyNot.1: Communication strategy is a valid consideration in 4.2.1, but it informs people rather than making the change last.
whyNot.2: Upskilling is also a valid consideration, but skills alone do not stop people drifting back to old habits.
whyNot.3: Stage tolerances control the project; they are not a consideration for embedding organizational change.

B.q: At Callowmere University, wellbeing staff have seen three earlier systems promised and dropped. The director proposes a launch email from the vice-chancellor and a cash bonus for staff who use the Student Support Hub in its first month. Which response BEST applies PRINCE2 Agile guidance on making the change stick?
options: Rely on the bonus, as rewards give the strongest push to adopt
Combine training, on-the-job coaching and an evolving culture
Rely on the launch email, as clear messages secure adoption
Make use of the hub compulsory and audit staff use monthly
B.why: People need theory training plus practical coaching on the job (2.7.3), and lasting change comes from an evolving culture (4.2.1). Incentives alone cannot guarantee that changes stay (4.5).

whyNot.0: Book 4.5 balances tangible incentives with purpose, recognition and personal values; a bonus by itself does not hold a change in place.
whyNot.2: Informing people is not enough: they need to understand and apply the change, which needs training and coaching.
whyNot.3: Compulsion and audits produce compliance while someone is watching; they do not evolve the culture.

C.q: Easterholm's leaders are used to fixed plans and some see agile as a way to avoid accountability. In initiating a project, the project manager writes the current state, an interim state in which practitioners join sprints for research and testing, the target state, and how practice champions and coaching will keep the new ways after closure. Is this an appropriate application of OCM, and why?
options: Yes, because it sets the route to the target state and how it will be kept
Yes, because it removes the need for a communication management approach
No, because a council new to agile needs an agile transformation plan
No, because OCM belongs to business as usual after the project closes
C.why: The change management approach can describe the target state and the interim states, and should consider the evolving culture and ways to stop changes being rolled back (4.2.1). This does both.

whyNot.1: The communication management approach is still agreed in initiating a project; the change management approach does not replace it.
whyNot.2: A transformation plan suits wider adoption across initiatives; for a single pilot, updating the change management approach is right.
whyNot.3: OCM is planned and led during the project; leaving it to business as usual risks the change never landing.

C.q: At Draycott Precision Engineering, several maintenance engineers say a computer cannot tell them when a machine will fail. The operations director plans to make the change stick by paying a bonus to each engineer who acts on dashboard alerts, with no other measures. Is this an appropriate way to embed the change, and why?
options: Yes, because tangible rewards help people adopt the agile values
Yes, because value-based incentives are a key agile consideration
No, because financial incentives alone cannot make the change last
No, because incentives belong in the commercial management approach
C.why: Book 4.5: financial or points incentives cannot guarantee that changes stay in place; they must be balanced with intangible motivators such as purpose and recognition, and with personal values. Lasting change needs an evolving culture (4.2.1).

whyNot.0: Tangible rewards can help, but as the sole measure they do not explain how this change will last.
whyNot.1: Value-based incentives are a 4.5 consideration, but this is a cash bonus with nothing else, so the verdict is wrong.
whyNot.3: The commercial management approach covers procurement and contracts, not staff motivation.

C.q: At Pinewick, the head of store operations proposes that once click and collect is live in a store, area managers check each week that staff follow the new process. Store adoption would be treated as complete when every store passes its first check. Is this an appropriate way to make the change last, and why?
options: Yes, because compliance checks prove that the target state is reached
Yes, because the stores will run the service as business as usual
No, because store staff should design the process before go-live
No, because compliance does not evolve the culture that keeps change
C.why: Making change last means evolving the culture and planning how changes will not be rolled back (4.2.1). Weekly compliance checks show behaviour while someone is watching; they do not change shared values and habits.

whyNot.0: Passing a check shows compliance at that moment, not a lasting change in how stores work.
whyNot.1: True that stores will run the service afterwards, which is exactly why the culture must change, not just the process.
whyNot.2: Involving store staff in design helps adoption, but it does not explain the flaw here: a passed compliance check is treated as lasting change.

reteach.title: A house move, not a parcel delivery
reteach.question: If a courier drops a new sofa at your door, has your family changed how it lives? What would it take?

blocks.body: A project is like a courier: it delivers products. Organizational change management is the house move: deciding where the family is going (target state), the stages on the way (interim states), and how everyone settles in so nobody drifts back to the old house. The change management approach is the moving plan for this project. If the whole street is moving over years, that bigger plan is the agile transformation plan.

steps.label: Learn and try
steps.sub: Training plus coaching on the job

blocks.text: A bonus, a rule or a launch email can get people through the door. Only an evolving culture keeps them living there. When a question asks what makes the change LAST, pick culture.

explain.body: OCM is the means by which an organization transitions from its current state to its target state. In an agile change, the target state includes the agile mindset and values in daily use. Without it, a project delivers products that people do not adopt, so benefits are not realized.

test.q: Saltmarsh's board asks the project manager what organizational change management will add to Repairs Reimagined. Which description should she give?
options: Controlling changes to the baselined project backlog
Setting the expected success level for each aspect
Moving the organization from current to target state
Planning several initiatives to adopt more agility
test.why: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current state to its target state (4.2.1).

whyNot.0: That is change control in the issues practice.
whyNot.1: That describes performance targets (1.3.2), not OCM.
whyNot.3: That describes an agile transformation plan (2.7.1), which is narrower than OCM.

explain.body: The change management approach describes this project's route from current to target state and is agreed in initiating a project. An agile transformation plan guides wider adoption of agility, usually across several initiatives, with goals tied to strategy. A single pilot updates the change management approach; where a transformation plan exists, it can replace the change management approach in the project initiation workshop.

test.q: Draycott has never used agile outside its software team. The board sees Smart Maintenance as a one-off pilot and has no wider adoption plan. Where should the move to agile ways of working for this project be planned?
options: In an agile transformation plan
In the change management approach
In the commercial management approach
In the project management team structure
test.why: For a single pilot, an agile transformation plan may not be needed yet; update the change management approach instead (2.7.1, 4.2.1).

whyNot.0: A transformation plan suits wider adoption across several initiatives; this is a one-off pilot.
whyNot.2: The commercial management approach covers procurement and the Senticore contract.
whyNot.3: The team structure covers who is involved and how they work together, not the organizational transition.

explain.body: When setting the detail of the change management approach, consider the communication strategy, learning and upskilling needs, and the evolving culture with ways to ensure changes are not rolled back. The last of these is what makes change last. Incentives alone cannot guarantee it: balance them with purpose, recognition and personal values.

test.q: At Callowmere, the project manager is setting the detail of the change management approach for the Student Support Hub. Which consideration does PRINCE2 Agile link to stopping the change being rolled back?
options: The evolving culture of the wellbeing service
The frequency of written reports to the board
The data protection officer's approval of data
The order of features in each planned release
test.why: Book 4.2.1 pairs the evolving culture with ways to ensure changes are not rolled back after the transformation.

whyNot.1: Reporting frequency is a progress matter, not a change management consideration.
whyNot.2: Data approval is a constraint on the product, not how the organizational change is embedded.
whyNot.3: Feature order is release planning in the plans practice.

explain.h: Agile ways of working help OCM
explain.body: Frequent releases make adoption incremental and smooth; users in the delivery team support organizational adoption; frequent testing raises user engagement; progress reviews with demos speed adoption; retrospectives at the end of each iteration capture lessons; regular feedback steers the product during iterations and after releases.

test.q: Callowmere's wellbeing staff are doubtful about the hub. Which action is MOST LIKELY to increase their engagement and speed up adoption?
options: Send staff a monthly written summary of progress
Bundle all features into one release in September
Use the team retrospective to track sprint progress
Demonstrate each increment to staff at progress reviews
test.why: Progress reviews that include demos increase user engagement and lead to faster adoption (4.2.4).

whyNot.0: Periodic reporting on its own is insufficient for communication and can be biased (4.4).
whyNot.1: Frequent releases support smooth adoption; one large release works against it.
whyNot.2: Retrospectives happen at the end of an iteration to learn lessons; they do not track progress during it.
